entries.title: There Are So Many Conspiracy Theories About Dolly Parton and Vaccines
entries.summary: Influential right-wing conspiracy theorists and MAGA-aligned pundits are falsely claiming that the Covid vaccine killed Dolly Parton, the vaccination advocate and philanthropist.
entries.content:
Conspiracy theories surrounding singer and philanthropist Dolly Parton’s recent death have flooded the internet, referencing everything from satanic rituals to cloning. But one conspiracy theory has dominated all the others: the claim that Parton’s death was caused by “turbo cancer” brought on by the Covid vaccine.

There is no evidence to support the claim that Parton’s death had anything to do with the vaccine. Parton, 80, died after “a short battle with cancer,” her family said in a statement. In May, Parton shared that she was responding well to treatment related to her immune system and digestive system.

In 2020, the singer donated $1 million to fund research in support of the vaccine. The following year, she filmed herself getting the vaccine, singing an adapted version of her hit song Jolene before receiving the shot. “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate," Parton sang in a video.

Now, a number of influential right-wing conspiracy theorists and MAGA-aligned pundits have spent the past few days claiming—or, in many cases, suggesting—that the vaccine killed Parton.

“Was Dolly Parton yet another Covid vaccine victim?” far-right radio host Wayne Allyn Root, who recently interviewed President Donald Trump on his show, wrote on X. "She took the vaxx on TV. She changed the name of her hit song 'Jolene Jolene' to 'Vaccine, Vaccine.' She encouraged fans to get it. Now she's dead of cancer. This sounds like another case of 'turbo cancer. RIP Dolly.” (Earlier this month, Root urged Trump to declare a national emergency during the midterms when he had the president on his show. “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” Trump responded.)

“Dolly Parton thought she was doing the right thing by backing the Moderna mRNA Covid shot,” Toby Rogers, who works with the Brownstone Institute, a think tank founded to oppose Covid restrictions and which has deep ties to the Trump administration, wrote on X. “But it very well may have killed her.” The Brownstone Institute was founded by Jeffrey Tucker, a close ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long undermined trust in a variety of vaccines.

While Kennedy has not commented publicly on Parton’s death, he has spent recent days blaming the Covid lockdowns for measles-related deaths, after the measles-related deaths of two unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania this week.

Valerie Anne Smith, a health influencer with 273,000 followers on X, shared multiple posts about Parton’s death, all of them suggesting that the Covid-19 vaccine was the cause of her death.

“Soon after being injected she developed severe autoimmune, liver and kidney issues,” Smith wrote. “Cause of death ... CANCER.”

“Dolly Parton was as universally beloved as a person can be,” Travis View, cohost of the QAnon Anonymous podcast, tells WIRED. “That’s exactly what made her a target for conspiracists online. Many anti-vaccine conspiracy theorists despised Parton because she not only encouraged others to get the vaccine, she even helped fund vaccine development.”

The conspiracy theories were not limited to X. Facebook was also flooded with wild allegations about Parton’s death, none of which provided any evidence to back up their claims.

One of the most popular themes focused on a video Parton made just weeks before her death in which she thanked pop star Taylor Swift and her husband, NFL star Travis Kelce, for their $2 million donation to Imagination Library, Parton’s childhood literacy charity. She jokingly also asked the couple if she could have their “firstborn” child.

The conspiracy theories focused on a brief moment in the video when Parton was moving her hands. Some social media users claimed that if paused, the video showed her making a “devil horns,” sign. The still image has been posted dozens of times on Facebook in recent days, garnering tens of thousands of likes and shares.

“Nothing to see here, folks, just Dolly Parton—the same woman who dropped $1 million to help fund the Moderna Covid vaccine—flashing devil horns while casually demanding Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s firstborn child,” an anonymous X account named Red Pill USA wrote, adding: “It’s a big Satanic club … and you ain’t in it.” The post has been viewed almost 1 million times.

On YouTube, conspiracy theorist David Nino Rodriguez, who has 613,000 followers, also referenced the Taylor Swift video and dedicated his show on Wednesday to claims that Parton’s death had been prophesied, and that it was a “marker for what comes next.”

“Some of these theories came specifically from her advocacy for the Covid vaccine and gay rights, and they're pretty rare when balanced with the outpouring of love,” Mike Rothschild, an author who writes about conspiracy theories, tells WIRED. “But a lot of what was said about Dolly was just standard-issue brain rot. There is a small part of the internet that now believes nobody dies without some involvement from the Covid vaccine, trafficking, or Satanism.”

entries.title: How an Atlanta Suburb Ended Up Sharing Flock Data With More Than 2,000 Organizations
entries.summary: Alpharetta, Georgia, cops share data with thousands of Flock users, ranging from federal agencies to a fish and wildlife commission. The reasons why show how vast—and invasive—the network has become.
entries.content:
Alpharetta, a prosperous suburb of Atlanta, Georgia, is home to about 67,000 people, served by about 120 local police officers. It also hosts several dozen cameras sold by Flock Safety, the increasingly controversial surveillance company that collects license plate data and other information and makes it searchable by police.

Data captured by those Flock cameras, WIRED has learned via public records requests, is accessible to more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, airports, and government agencies across the United States. These range from Morehouse College to Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Commission and include Medicare fraud investigators in Illinois, a drug task force focused on east-central Missouri, and the inspector general of a federal agency.

In return, Alpharetta receives Flock data from more than 1,300 entities, which span from the prosecutor’s office of Whitley County, Indiana, to the Metro Police Authority of Genesee County, Michigan.

The Alpharetta Police Department—which, as reported by WIRED, had an officer resign due to Flock misuse on August 5—also exchanges Flock data with several agencies that have been similarly rocked by recent incidents of officers misusing its technology, including Georgia’s Bibb County Sheriff’s Department, the Savannah Police Department, and the Dallas Police Department.

Alpharetta’s data-sharing network has expanded tremendously over the past year. Since June 2025, the number of entities receiving data from Alpharetta police has grown by about 42 percent, and the number of entities sending data to them has grown by about 125 percent. And, according to documents obtained via public records requests from several other cities around the country, Alpharetta is far from alone in having an expansive and complicated data-sharing system, providing a potent example of how pervasive Flock’s surveillance network has become.

One of Flock’s central selling points is its network of customers—mostly, though not entirely, law enforcement agencies. If a criminal suspect crosses city, county, or perhaps state lines, Flock tells its customers, a query can prevent them from falling through the cracks.

Data sharing across agencies is hardly novel. A police department can, for instance, share data from its automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) with state-run fusion centers, which centralize resources from law enforcement agencies in particular regions. They could also share it with a regional High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program. (Alpharetta police agreed to do just that in 2025, according to a memorandum of understanding that WIRED obtained.)

Whereas HIDTAs are federally funded public programs, Flock is a private company that manages a sprawling, interconnected ALPR network governed by rules and restrictions that vary wildly from city to city. And if police departments don’t closely supervise their settings for data requests and sharing within Flock’s interface, they can unwittingly become nodes in a much larger surveillance network than they necessarily know or understand.

This can lead to situations like that in Alpharetta, where citizens and visitors are embedded in a data-sharing network that has propagated to more than 2,300 nodes. So, how does it happen?

Setting Boundaries

To understand how cities like Alpharetta can build such expansive data-sharing networks with Flock, it’s important to understand how Flock’s interface actually works.

WIRED analyzed a cache of files on Flock’s website that are served by its login pages to anyone who loads them. Some of the code that WIRED analyzed illustrates what a Flock administrator might see in their own Flock interface—specifically, in their settings and sharing preferences.

An administrator can automatically share their agency’s Flock data with any organization within a custom radius, within their home state, or within one or more other states. Alternatively, they can individually choose organizations to share data with.

Administrators can also limit specific data that other organizations can receive, like live or archived videos. They can also limit which organizations can ask them for data. They could restrict this, for instance, to organizations based in the same state, or within a 50-mile radius.

Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that per the city’s Flock settings, the department will “automatically approve” requests for its Flock data from law enforcement agencies within 500 miles. If they’re outside that radius, the police department has to individually request access to Alpharetta’s data.

Hiott was unable to say what the Alpharetta police department’s default settings were, whether it altered the default settings, or how long the radius has been set to 500 miles—though he did note that the department “does not share any live feeds, analytics, etc. with anyone.”

Flock spokesperson Jess Montejano claims that data sharing is turned off by default for new and onboarding customers—so no law enforcement agencies automatically get access to another agency’s data. Flock did not specify whether that has always been the case.

Paris Lewbel, another Flock spokesperson, adds that “historically,” its customers have been able to request data from other customers that are within the same state, or within 50 miles—the precursor to actually sharing data.

Coast-to-Coast

Flock’s network settings allow agencies to set specific limits on what Flock data it shares and receives, but in some cases, police departments have been caught off guard by how expansive the search settings were for their officers.

Often, the confusion has been tied to Flock’s Nationwide Lookup tool, which the company introduced in 2023. It allows any Flock customer to query any other Flock customer in the country, as long as they have a specific license plate. (Flock disabled the tool for federal agencies following backlash to the company’s pilot program with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.) In several cases, Flock customers had no idea this tool was enabled.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former police officer, government official, or Flock Safety employee who wants to talk about the company? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.

Chris Shook is the city attorney in Reynoldsburg, Ohio, where two officers recently resigned after the police department probed their alleged misuse of Flock’s technology. He tells WIRED that in June, the city’s police department made an unexpected discovery while attempting to complete a public records request: Per the department’s Flock settings, the Nationwide Lookup tool was active. Police leadership, however, had been under the impression that officers could only search cameras within Ohio.

Shook says that the police department immediately changed the settings to enable only in-state camera searches. But they had no idea when, or why, nationwide searches may have been enabled. Lacking answers, Shook turned to Flock.

According to emails reviewed by WIRED, Flock public affairs manager Caroline Bush could only say that Nationwide Lookup “was enabled at some point before February 2025.” Due to an “event-log limitation” prior to that month, she could not say exactly when. But she added that, upon checking the police department’s audit, she “found nationwide searches as early as 03/2023.”

This came as a surprise to Shook. If nationwide search was enabled, he said, there must have been an error, “but we are unsure of how that error could have occurred.”

“The most likely explanation is that the setting was enabled during initial account setup or onboarding,” Bush replied. She said Nationwide Lookup “was a common default configuration for agencies at that time, before Flock introduced stronger in-product disclosures and tighter controls around this feature.”

In California, the Palo Alto Police Department had a similar experience. In a city council “study session” led by city manager Ed Shikada on June 1, he claimed that Flock activated Nationwide Lookup “for all customers” in mid-2023. But notably, California law forbids sharing ALPR data with federal or out-of-state law enforcement. He says that Flock quietly "disabled" Nationwide Lookup for Palo Alto police in October 2024, and for all California law enforcement by March 2025.

However, Shikada said Palo Alto police didn't know Nationwide Lookup had ever been active until December 2025. Flock did not respond to requests for comment regarding its National Lookup tool ahead of publication.

Meanwhile, Commander David Hart of Minnesota’s Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office tells WIRED that while his office didn’t have a debacle with the Nationwide Lookup tool, he had to reel in the permissions that were set up when the county started using Flock in early 2024.

For the first few months, his officers could send and receive data requests to any Flock customer in the country. But toward the end of 2024, Hart says, he limited outgoing and incoming data requests to in-state agencies. No data requests are approved automatically. (Minnesota’s ALPR statute sets specific standards that agencies must meet before capturing or receiving ALPR data.) Hart tells WIRED that on principle, he doesn’t believe in using Flock casually for wide-ranging searches.

“It’s gotten to the point where people want to search more agencies just to be able to search more agencies, without a real reason behind it,” Hart says.

When examining Flock audit logs, it’s not always obvious why an officer would want or need to expand the scope of their search.

WIRED filed a public records request to the Reynoldsburg Police Department and received 549 pages that log every Flock query its officers made from January 2024 through April 2026. The records show that even from query to query, the number of probed Flock networks can vary significantly.

On January 1, 2025, for instance, a Reynoldsburg police officer queried 53 Flock networks. The officer’s “reason” for the search, according to the log, was a potential criminal offense coded “30.” Just 40 minutes later, the same officer cited the same criminal offense code but, for reasons the log does not specify, instead queried 5,392 Flock networks. Similar examples appear regularly throughout the log, though most of the searches WIRED reviewed had probed fewer than 100 networks.

Flock users, as illustrated in a recent video on the company’s YouTube channel, can customize the number of networks they want to probe in a single query. A police officer can probe every single camera network their department has access to—or they can limit their search to their state, or simply their own jurisdiction. That decision is left up to the officer.

“The particular officer can narrow the networks they want to search, but typically they don't,” Shook tells WIRED. “Typically, they search every network they have access to.”

Mixed Company

Alpharetta’s Flock data-sharing network shows that it sends data to and receives it from agencies that, along with being geographically distant, are a far cry from the local police departments and county sheriff offices that represent Flock’s prototypical customers.

It’s often unclear, outside of a fluke circumstance, what the agencies would gain from exchanging data.

For instance, it’s not obvious why the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration, Region G of the Alabama Drug Enforcement Task Force, or the University of North Texas’ Denton campus police would need to have a mutual exchange of Flock data with the police department of Alpharetta, Georgia. (None of these agencies responded to requests for comment.)

WIRED contacted more than a dozen agencies sending or receiving data with the Alpharetta Police that are neither a police department nor a sheriff’s office, and most did not respond to requests for comment. Just one answered specific questions about its use of Flock: Kentucky’s Louisville Regional Airport Authority, a nearly seven-hour drive from Alpharetta.

Natalie Ciresi Chaudoin, the airport authority’s director of public relations, tells WIRED that the Louisville Regional Airport Authority has 13 Flock cameras across its properties. She says that the airport shares data from its cameras with 2,240 federal, state, and local agencies across the country and receives data from 1,124 agencies.

Chaudoin adds that the airport’s Flock settings are configured to “automatically accept a request for data-sharing with in-state law enforcement agencies, while out-of-state agencies’ requests are manually accepted or declined following their review.”

When asked about Alpharetta, Chaudoin says that the airport was “aware that it received data from an agency” in the city. The airport has not shared its data in return.

Limiting Factors

Twenty-four states, as well as Washington, DC, have statutes covering ALPR use. The regulations they impose differ widely from state to state, with some being quite specific: Since 2023, it’s been illegal for law enforcement in Illinois to use ALPR data in criminal cases related to immigration or abortion.

The effects of California’s restrictions are visible in records obtained via public records request from the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC), which are published publicly on Muckrock, a public records request facilitator. According to the records, the fusion center shares and receives data from fewer than 400 agencies—a fraction of the agencies in Alpharetta’s network—and they’re all based in California. However, that fact alone doesn’t paint the whole picture.

According to an audit of searches run on the NCRIC’s Flock network, NCRIC member agencies ran more than 57,000 Flock queries in the single month between November 26 and December 26, 2025. Many of the queries probed thousands of Flock networks, and more than 96 percent of them probed at least 100.

In other words, the scope of the NCRIC queries tended to be significantly larger than those of the Reynoldsburg Police Department—the police department in a state with no ALPR statute, where officers had access to the Nationwide Lookup tool until June and from which two officers recently resigned due to allegedly misusing Flock.

On August 13, Flock announced a set of changes to how its software works, seemingly in response to a surge in news coverage about police officers misusing the technology. The company said that it is now “recommending a 7-day ALPR data retention period,” a reduction from 30 days. But Flock customers can pay for extended data retention, according to documents obtained via a public records request from St. Petersburg, Florida.

Flock also says that law enforcement can’t run a Flock search without entering a criminal case code and that by the end of the year, all customers must activate its Audit Assistance tool, which scans for “defined criteria for abnormal behavior” and “automatically” suspends Flock access if detected.

In Alpharetta, according to Lieutenant Hiott, police chief Trent Lindgren learned about the Audit Assistance tool in July and promptly activated it. By July 20, the department had opened an investigation into one of its officers. On August 5, the officer resigned.

entries.title: Uber Eats Promo Codes: $15 Off │September 2026

entries.content:

Then in 2014, Uber leveled up with Uber Eats. Much like Uber was the convenient, modern answer to taxis, Uber Eats was the equivalent to the world of food delivery.

Instead of calling a local restaurant and enlisting a delivery driver from said restaurant, Uber Eats draws from hundreds of participating restaurants, cafes, and stores from your local region, tailoring deals and picks based on your location and preference. So if you want fresh sushi from your favorite local spot for a date-night in, or just need some Advil and Gatorade after a night out, Uber Eats delivers you the goods in minutes flat. Whether you’re new to the service, or an old devotee, we have an Uber Eats promo code and other Uber Eats coupon codes to help you save big—and stay at home.

One of the easiest ways to save major coin with Uber Eats is by creating a new account. First-time Uber customers can save 30 to 50% on their initial order, including new offers with up to $20 off rides, or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber Eats promo code to get this steep discount—this Uber Eats discount applies automatically when you create your account and book your first trip or delivery.

If you’re someone who uses the rideshare app often or orders take out multiple nights a week, an Uber One membership will pay for itself within a few weeks. You’ll get tons of perks across rides and food delivery, like $0 delivery fees on eligible food, grocery, and retail orders, up to 10% off eligible Uber Eats orders, 5% back in Uber One credits on eligible rides, and automatic surge savings. Uber One members save $29 on average every month.

Like I said above, the simplest way to save big with Uber is if you’re a first-time user. You’ll save 30 to 50% on your initial ride, including up to $20 off all rides, or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber promo code, Uber welcome discounts apply automatically once you create your account and book your first trip. Trust, you’ll get used to the convenience of a rideshare app, along with a food and delivery service app all in one convenient place—in the palm of your hand.

Share the Gift of an Uber Eats Gift Card

One of my go-to gifts recently is an Uber Eats gift card. I find it’s especially thoughtful and useful as a gift of convenience, whether that’s after a death, loss, birth, or big life change. An Uber Eats gift card is more than just a gift card, it’s taking another thing to worry about off someone’s plate, it’s providing an easy, comforting meal, especially in times of grief or celebration. Uber gift cards start at $15 and can be purchased from participating retailers, or sent instantly through the app to friends and family members.

Unlock an Uber Eats Student Discount

Being a student means tight budgets, long nights, and often limited kitchen space (and culinary knowledge). Investing in an Uber One account may be a good idea—for only $10 per month you can get, on average, $30 in savings per month on Uber rides and Uber grocery and meal delivery. You won’t have to worry about planning meals or expensive takeout bills, by using Uber One discounts and promos, you can get multiple meals for the week for less. No Uber Eats coupon code necessary, just verify your student status to get the four weeks for free and $5 per month after.

If you’re not feeling like eating out, stay in and get groceries delivered with Uber Eats. Uber has hundreds of participating grocery stores near you—including your favorite supermarkets and grocery stores for same day delivery in as little as 25 minutes. By using your location, they have options for fast delivery from drugstores, grocery chains, and local stores so whether you need some toilet paper or a gallon of milk, Uber Eats delivers.

Deliver With Uber Eats

If you’re looking for a side hustle or want gig work where you make your own schedule, delivering with Uber Eats is a great way to earn extra cash. It's flexible in so many ways, you can deliver with a car, a bike, or on foot, for an hour, a day, or daily. Uber Eats makes it easy to know what you’ll be making and what your day will look like. You’ll be able to see how much you’ll earn by delivering before you accept a job, and the tips you get are all yours. With Instant Pay, you can cash out up to 6 times a day for a fee, and weekly earnings are automatically transferred to your bank account. The possibilities (and flexibility) are endless—you can sign up to deliver food and packages, as well as “Shop & Deliver,” which allows you to earn by shopping for customers and delivering the order.

entries.content:
If you’ve been outside, to the gym, or on a basketball court, there’s a good chance you’ve seen someone wearing Reeboks. The brand has had its fair share of ups and downs, but is riding a wave of increased interest driven by smart business moves like a refocus on sports and lifestyle, alongside a number of high-profile collaborations like the Reebok G-Unit G6 50 Cent.

Founded in 1958, Reebok has changed hands and gone through multiple iterations. Most recently in 2022, Reebok was sold by Adidas to Authentic Brands Group for over two billion dollars. Since then, it’s reinvigorated its sports lineup, hired Shaquel O’ Neal as president of Reebok basketball, and signed tons of professional athletes across basketball, golf, and tennis to the brand.

But what about the shoes? They’re solid. As someone who used to test training and running shoes, the Reebok Floatzig and Reebok Nano X series are excellent performers for the price—I still wear my Nano X4s anytime I’m strength training. Other standouts include the more lifestyle oriented Classic and Club lineups.

But given how often you should replace sneakers (hint: often every six months), you should always look for a deal when shopping. That’s why I rounded up some of the best Reebok coupons and Reebok promo codes below, to help you save time and money.

Use this Reebok Promo Code for up to $30 off

The more you spend on Reebok’s site, the more potential savings you can get when you shop its Buy More, Save More section. This collection has over 1,000 pieces of shoes and apparel, including popular styles like the Club and Nano series, so you can probably find something fitting. You get $10 off orders of $100 or more, $20 off $150 orders, and $30 off orders of $200 or more using the Reebok discount code BMSM at checkout.

15% Reebok Discount Code for New Customers

Anyone making a new account at Reebok online or the Reebok app can get 15% off their first purchase using the Reebok discount code MOVE15. This Reebok promo code works after you sign up for a new account and verify your email address, and is applied automatically at checkout if you are using the Reebok app. Standard exclusions to select collaboration items and limited-edition sneaker releases apply, so double check your order before purchase to make sure you qualify for the Reebok coupon code deal.

You also get access to early product drops, sale alerts, and birthday rewards. This perk is applied automatically when logged in using Shop Pay at checkout. An Authentics membership also gives you discounts at other participating brands like Champion, Billabong, Hunter, Ted Baker, and more, so it’s worth considering, especially if you shop multiple brands. This Reebok discount is for online purchases only.

Stack Reebok Coupons with Clearance and Seasonal Sales for up to 50% More Off

It’s easy to stack savings with Reebok if you know where to look. Items in season sales like Back to School or just the regular Reebok clearance section can be discounted by as much as 65%. Add extra discounts (and free shipping) from an Authentics Membership, plus Bundle & Save offers, and you can drop the price of your checkout cart dramatically, without needing a Reebok discount code.

Double check your code before looking elsewhere—it could be you just have a typo.

entries.title: A Judge Has Blocked the Pentagon’s Attempt to Blacklist Anthropic
entries.summary: A federal judge has called the Department of Defense’s designation of Anthropic as a national security supply-chain risk “illegal and baseless.”
entries.content:
A federal judge on Thursday barred the Trump administration from designating Anthropic a national security risk over a dispute about the use of its AI models, ruling that the designation amounted to unconstitutional retaliation.

The decision handed down by US district judge Rita Lin in California vacated the February 27 decision by defense secretary Pete Hegseth to label Anthropic a “supply-chain risk” and make the company ineligible for federal contracts. The ruling also lifted an additional punitive measure by Hegseth that prevented contractors or suppliers to the US military from doing business with Anthropic, a position Lin called “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law.”

“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless,” Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling.

The judge also ruled that nine agencies—including the Pentagon, the Treasury Department, the State Department, and the Department of Homeland Security—had improperly imposed sanctions on Anthropic. The ruling removes those penalties.

However, Lin affirmed that the Pentagon is not required to use Anthropic’s models, and the ruling does not prevent the Pentagon from electing to simply use other models. A Pentagon spokesperson could not immediately be reached for comment, but the department is expected to appeal.

In a statement, Anthropic spokesperson Danielle Cohen said, “We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply-chain risk designation was unlawful. We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security.”

The case stems from a bitter dispute earlier this year between the Pentagon and Anthropic over a $200 million deal to use the AI lab’s Claude models for military applications.

The rift began after reports that the US had used Claude in the operation to capture Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. After the operation, a Palantir employee relayed concerns from an Anthropic staffer to US officials about how its models had been used.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Trump administration employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at hugolowell.15.

In negotiations, Anthropic insisted on certain limits on how its models could be deployed, including support for lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance systems. But Hegseth rejected any curbs, contending that a contractor could not dictate how the technology could be used once deployed and insisting the contract allowed “all lawful use.”

After negotiations broke down in February, Hegseth was widely seen as punishing Anthropic by designating it a “supply-chain risk,” a national security tool that blacklisted the company from doing business with the federal government.

The Pentagon said at the time that the supply-chain risk label was appropriate, because giving Anthropic access to any classified systems would “introduce unacceptable risk” if the AI lab could disable or alter its technology, for instance, at a time of war.

Anthropic filed two lawsuits in response—one in federal district court in California and one at the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia—accusing the Pentagon of violating its First and Fifth Amendment protections on ideological grounds. The DC case is ongoing.

Anthropic’s top AI models are considered some of the best in the world. Separate from the supply chain risk designation, Anthropic's models recently became subject to the Trump administration’s AI oversight framework due to their powerful capabilities.

Lin cited the administration’s involvement in reviewing advanced Anthropic models as part of her ruling. “Even now, the government is discussing collaboration with Anthropic on its new model, Mythos, in an array of sensitive contexts,” she wrote. “None of that is consistent with a genuine fear that Anthropic is a saboteur who would poison its software to harm national security.”

Additional reporting by Maxwell Zeff.
